'I seek refuge in Allah with that by which Musa, Isa and Ibrahim, who fulfilled, sought refuge, from the evil of what He created, multiplied and originated, and from the evil of Iblis and his armies, and from the evil of what transgresses.

'I seek refuge in Allah, the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing, from the accursed Satan: ﴿By those ranked in rows, and those who drive with firm driving, and those who recite the reminder: indeed your God is One, Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them, and Lord of the easts. Indeed, We have adorned the nearest heaven with an adornment of stars, and as protection from every rebellious devil. They cannot listen to the exalted assembly, and they are pelted from every side, repelled, and for them is a perpetual punishment. Except one who snatches a fragment, and he is pursued by a piercing flame.﴾'"

This is some of what relates to his ﷺ saying regarding that servant: "He protects himself from the devil by remembering Allah the Exalted."

(Section)
Among His names is "the King" (al-Malik). The true meaning of kingship belongs to Him, Glorified is He, in every respect, and this attribute necessarily entails all the other attributes of perfection. For it is impossible for complete and true kingship to be established for one who has no life, no power, no will, no hearing, no sight, no speech, and no voluntary action proceeding from him. How can one be described as a king who does not command or forbid, does not reward or punish, does not give or withhold, does not honour or abase, does not humble or dignify, does not bestow favour or take vengeance, does not raise or lower, does not send messengers to the regions of his kingdom, and does not direct his servants with his commands and prohibitions? What true kingship is there for one who lacks all of that? This shows that those who deny His names and attributes (al-mu'attilah) have made His subjects more perfect than He is, and one of them would be averse to having his own command and kingship described in the way he describes his Lord. Thus the attribute of divine kingship necessitates the existence of what the exercise of kingship cannot be complete without, and all of it comes from Him, Glorified is He. So the perfection of His kingship does not depend on anything other than Him, for everything else is attributed to Him and depends for its existence on His will and His creation.

(Section)
Ibn al-Qayyim said, after some discussion:
Once you understand these two points, applying the name "al-Salam" (the Giver of Peace, the Free from Imperfection) to God as one of His names is more fitting than all of that and more deserving of this name than any other bearer of it, because He, Glorified is He, is free from every defect and deficiency in every respect. He is the true Peace in every sense, whereas the created being is peaceful only in a relative sense. He, Glorified is He, is "Peace" in His essence, free from every defect and deficiency one might imagine; He is "Peace" in His attributes, free from every defect and deficiency; and He is "Peace" in His actions, free from every defect, evil, injustice, or act that occurs without wisdom. Rather, He is the true Peace in every respect and in every sense. It is thus known that His deserving this name is more complete than the deserving of anything else to which it is applied. This is the reality of the transcendence (tanzih) with which He has declared Himself transcendent and with which His Messenger declared Him transcendent. He is "Peace" from having a consort or a child, "Peace" from having an equal, a peer, a namesake, or a like, and "Peace" from having a partner. Therefore, when you consider the individual attributes of His perfection, you will find that each attribute is a "peace" from what contradicts its perfection. His life is peace from death, from drowsiness and sleep. Likewise His self-subsistence (qayyumiyyah) and His power are peace from fatigue and weariness. His knowledge is peace from anything being absent from it, from the onset of forgetfulness, or from any need for recollection or reflection. His will is peace from departing from wisdom and benefit. His words are peace from falsehood and injustice; indeed His words are complete in truthfulness and justice. His self-sufficiency (ghina) is peace from any need for another in any respect; rather everything else is in need of Him while He is free from everything other than Him. His kingship is peace from any contender for it, any partner, any helper who is a supporter, or any intercessor with Him without His permission. His divinity is peace from any partner in it; rather He is Allah, there is no god but He. His forbearance, pardon, forgiveness, and overlooking are peace from being due to any need of His, or to any flattery, or to any obsequiousness, as happens with others; rather they are pure generosity, benevolence, and munificence. Likewise His punishment, vengeance, severity of seizing, and swiftness of retribution are peace from being injustice, gloating, harshness, or cruelty; rather they are pure wisdom, justice, and the placing of things in their proper places. These too deserve praise and thanks just as His benevolence, reward, and blessings do. Indeed, if He were to place reward where punishment belongs, that would contradict His wisdom and His might. So His placing punishment where it belongs is part of His justice, wisdom, and might.

He is peace from what His enemies and those ignorant of Him imagine of contradiction to His wisdom, His decree, and His destiny. He is peace from futility, oppression, and injustice, and from the supposition that anything occurs contrary to His profound wisdom, and from His legislation and His religion. He is peace from contradiction, disagreement, instability, and anything contrary to the benefit and mercy of His servants, to doing good to them, and to His wisdom. Rather, all of His legislation is wisdom, mercy, benefit, and justice. Likewise, His giving is peace from being an exchange or from any need of the giver; and His withholding is peace from stinginess and fear of poverty. Rather, His giving is pure benevolence, not for exchange nor out of need, and His withholding is pure justice and wisdom, unmixed with stinginess or incapacity.

His istiwa' (rising) and His exaltation over His Throne are peace from being in need of what would bear Him or what He would rise upon. Rather, the Throne is in need of Him, and its bearers are in need of Him; He is free of the Throne, of its bearers, and of everything other than Him. His istiwa' and His exaltation are not confined by any limit, nor by any need for a Throne or anything else, nor by anything encompassing Him, Glorified and Exalted is He. Rather, He was (and there was no Throne), and He had no need of it, and He is the Self-Sufficient, the Praiseworthy. His istiwa' over His Throne and His dominion over His creation are among the requirements of His kingship and His subjugation, without any need for an accident or anything else in any respect. His descent every night to the lowest heaven is peace from what contradicts His exaltation, and peace from what contradicts His self-sufficiency. His perfection is peace from everything that a denier (mu'attil) or an anthropomorphist (mushabbih) might imagine. It is peace from ever being beneath anything or confined within anything.

Exalted is our Lord above everything that contradicts His perfection, His self-sufficiency, His hearing, and His sight, peace from everything that the anthropomorphist imagines or the denier invents, and His allegiance to His friends (muwalah).

It is peace from His allegiance being like the allegiance of one created to another created. Rather, it is an allegiance of mercy, goodness, benevolence, and kindness, as He said: ﴿And say: "Praise be to God, who has not taken a son, and who has no partner in the dominion, and who has no protecting friend out of weakness."﴾

So He did not negate that He may have a friend absolutely; rather He negated that He have a friend out of weakness. Likewise His love for those who love Him and for His friends is peace from the accidents of a created being's love for another created being, such as being love from need, or flattery, or benefit from being near to them. It is also peace from what the deniers say about it. Likewise what He attributed to Himself, such as a hand and a face: it is peace from what the anthropomorphist imagines or the denier invents.

So reflect on how His name "al-Salam" comprises all that He has declared Himself transcendent of, Blessed and Exalted is He. How many are those who have memorized this name without knowing what these secrets and meanings it contains. And God is the One sought for help, and the One asked to grant success in commenting on the Most Beautiful Names in this manner; He is near and responsive.

(Section)
Among His names, Exalted is He, is "al-Mu'min." It means, according to one of the two interpretations, the one who confirms the truthfulness of the truthful by establishing for them the evidences of their truthfulness. He is the One who confirmed His messengers and prophets in what they conveyed from Him, and bore witness for them that they are truthful by means of the proofs by which He demonstrated their truthfulness, both by decree and by creation. For He, Glorified is He, has informed us, and His information is truth and His word is the truth, that the servants will surely see among the signs upon the horizons and within themselves what makes clear to them that the revelation conveyed by His messengers is true. He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿We will show them Our signs in the horizons and within themselves until it becomes clear to them that it is the truth﴾ [Fussilat: 53], i.e., the Qur'an. For it is the one referred to earlier in His saying: ﴿Say: "Have you considered: if it is from God and you disbelieve in it..."﴾ [Fussilat: 52]. Then He said: ﴿Is it not sufficient concerning your Lord that He is a witness over all things?﴾ [Fussilat: 53]. So He, Glorified is He, bore witness to His Messenger by His saying that what he brought is the truth, and promised him that He would show the servants, from His signs in creation and action, what bears witness to that as well. Then He mentioned what is greater and more majestic than that: His witnessing over all things. For among His names is al-Shahid (the Witness), who is never absent from anything, and from whom not an atom's weight is hidden in the earth or in the heaven. Rather, He is aware of everything, present to everything, knowing its details. This is an argument from His names and attributes; the first is an argument from His speech and words, and argument from the signs upon the horizons and within the self is an argument from His actions and creatures.

If you say: "I have understood argument from His words and argument from His creatures; so explain to me how to argue from His names and attributes, for that is something we have no familiarity with in our discourse and books."

I say: Indeed! By God's life, it is as you have said, and its matter is more majestic and more exalted. For the Lord, Exalted is He, is the One indicated, and His signs are the evidence and proof.

Know that God, Glorified is He, in reality is the One who indicates Himself through His signs. He is in reality the guide for His servants through what He has established for them of indications and signs. He has deposited in the natural dispositions (fitar) that have not been defiled by denial and rejection that He, Glorified is He, is perfect in His names and attributes, and that He is described with every perfection, free from every defect and deficiency. So all life belongs to Him, all knowledge belongs to Him, all power belongs to Him, and hearing, sight, will, desire, mercy, self-sufficiency, generosity, benevolence, and righteousness all belong exclusively to Him and subsist in Him. What of His perfection is hidden from creatures is far greater and far greater than what they know of it; rather there is no proportion between what they know of that and what they do not know.

And of His sacred perfection is His awareness of everything and His witnessing over it, such that no aspect of the details of anything is hidden from Him, nor any atom of its particles, outwardly or inwardly. For one whose state is this, how is it fitting for servants to associate others with Him, to worship others alongside Him, or to make another god alongside Him? Rather, He must make him an example for His servants, as His practice has run concerning those who fabricate against Him. Here the answer to the conditional ends, and then He reports a definite, unconditional statement: that He ﴿will erase falsehood and establish the truth﴾ [al-Shura: 24].

So He informed that whoever negates from Him sending messengers and speech has not measured Him with His true measure, has not known Him as He should be known, and has not glorified Him as He deserves. Likewise, He is argued for by His names and attributes for His oneness and for the invalidity of polytheism, as in His saying:

﴿He is God, other than whom there is no god, Knower of the unseen and the witnessed; He is the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful. He is God, other than whom there is no god, the King, the Most Holy, the Peace, the Giver of Security, the Guardian, the Almighty, the Compeller, the Supreme. (Section)
As for al-Jabbar among the names of the Lord, Exalted is He: it has been explained as the One who mends the broken and enriches the poor, and the Lord, Glorified is He, is indeed so, but this is not the meaning of His name al-Jabbar. For this reason He paired it with His name al-Mutakabbir (the Supremely Great). Rather, it is "al-Jabarut" (dominion and majesty), and the Prophet ﷺ used to say:

"Glory be to the One of dominion, sovereignty, greatness, and magnificence."

So al-Jabbar is a name of glorification, like al-Mutakabbir, al-Malik, al-'Azim, and al-Qahhar. Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿al-Jabbar, al-Mutakabbir﴾, said: "He is the Mighty." And "jabarut" of God is His magnificence. "Jabbar" is also one of the names of kings, and "al-jabr" means the king, and "al-jababirah" means the kings. A poet said:

"And good morning, O you kings"

i.e., O you kings.

Al-Suddi said: "He is the One who compels people and forces them to what He wills." So according to this, al-Jabbar means al-Qahhar.

Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: "He was named al-Jabbar only because He compelled creation to what He willed, and creatures are too lowly in their affairs to disobey their Lord for the blink of an eye except by His will."

Al-Zajjaj said: "al-Jabbar is the One who compelled creation to what He willed."

Ibn al-Anbari said: "al-Jabbar in the description of the Lord, Glorified is He, is the One who cannot be attained."

From this is the saying "a jabbarah palm tree," when it is beyond the reach of the one who would grasp it. So al-Jabbar in the description of the Lord, Glorified is He, refers back to three meanings: (dominion, subjugation, and loftiness). For when a palm tree grows tall and rises, beyond the reach of hands, it is called jabbarah. For this reason He, Glorified is He, made His name al-Jabbar paired with al-'Aziz (the Mighty) and al-Mutakabbir, and each of these three names includes the other two.

These three names are parallel to three other names: (al-Khaliq, al-Bari', al-Musawwir: the Creator, the Originator, the Fashioner). So al-Jabbar and al-Mutakabbir operate as an elaboration of the meaning of the name al-'Aziz, just as al-Bari' and al-Musawwir are an elaboration of the meaning of the name al-Khaliq. Thus al-Jabbar among His attributes returns to the perfection of power, might, and dominion, and for this reason it is among His Most Beautiful Names.

As for the created being, his being described as jabbar is a blame and a deficiency, as God, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Thus God seals every heart of a proud tyrant﴾ [Ghafir: 35].

And God, Exalted is He, said to His Messenger ﷺ: ﴿You are not over them a jabbar﴾ [Qaf: 45], i.e., one who dominates them, compelling and forcing them to belief.

In al-Tirmidhi and others, from the Prophet ﷺ: "The tyrants and the arrogant will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection in the form of ants, trampled upon by people."

As for "al-Khaliq" (the Creator) and "al-Musawwir" (the Fashioner): if they are used absolutely, without qualification, they are applied only to the Lord, as in His saying: ﴿the Creator, the Originator, the Fashioner﴾. If they are used with a qualification, they may be applied to a servant, as one says to someone who measures something out for its cutting: that he creates it. A poet said:

"And you indeed cut what you have created, while some people create and then do not cut."

Ibn al-Qayyim's commentary on surah 59, verses 23–24 (part 2 of 2):

That is, you have a power by which you carry out and execute what you have decreed in yourself and in others. Someone may decree things while being unable to carry them out and enforce them. In this sense, it is valid to apply the term "creator" (khaliq) to a servant, in the words of the Exalted: ﴿So blessed is Allah, the best of creators﴾.

That is, the best of those who shape and those who determine. The Arabs say "qaddartu al-adim wa khalaqtuhu" ("I measured the leather and cut it") when one measures a hide in order to cut from it a water-skin, a waterskin (qirba), or the like.

Mujahid said: "They create, and Allah creates, and Allah is the best of creators."

Al-Layth said: "A man who is a khaliq is one who makes (sani'), and the women are al-khaliqat."

Muqatil said: "The Exalted says: He is better in creation than those who make images and other things, of which nothing moves. As for al-Bari' (the Originator), it is not valid to apply it to anyone except Him, the Glorified, for He is the one who originated (bara'a) creation and brought it into being after it was non-existent."

The servant's power does not extend to that, for the furthest reach of his capacity is to manipulate some attributes of what the Lord, the Exalted, has brought into being and originated, and to change them from one state to another in a specific manner beyond which his power does not extend.

Not from this category is "bara'tu al-qalam" (I trimmed the pen), because it is a defective (mu'tall) root, not a hamzated one; nor is "bara'tu min al-maradh" (I recovered from the illness), because it is an intransitive verb, not transitive. Likewise, "mubdi' al-shay'" (the originator of a thing) and "badi'uhu" (its innovator/wonderful maker) are not valid to apply except to the Lord, as in His saying: ﴿Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾.

Ibداع (al-ibda', innovation/origination) is bringing a thing into being without a precedent example. A servant is called mubtadi' (an innovator) because he has introduced a statement that was not practiced by the Sunnah. Then whoever follows him in it is also called mubtadi'.

(Benefit)

Know that He, the Glorified, uses His names to prove His oneness and to negate association with Him. Had these been names without meaning, they would not indicate this, as in the saying of Harun to the worshippers of the calf: ﴿O my people, you are only being tested by it, and indeed your Lord is the Most Merciful﴾ [Ta-Ha: 90].

And His saying, in the same story: ﴿Your god is only Allah, other than whom there is no deity, who has encompassed all things in knowledge﴾ [Ta-Ha: 98].

And His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And your God is one God; there is no deity except Him, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate﴾ [al-Baqarah: 163].

And His saying, the Glorified, at the end of Surah al-Hashr: ﴿He is Allah, other than whom there is no deity, the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed; He is the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. He is Allah, other than whom there is no deity, the King, the Pure, the Source of Peace, the Granter of Security, the Guardian, the Mighty, the Compeller, the Superior. Glory be to Allah above what they associate with Him﴾ [al-Hashr: 22–23].

So "sabbaha" (glorified) means He declared Himself free of the associations of the polytheists with Him, right after praising Himself with His most beautiful names, which necessitate His oneness and the impossibility of affirming a partner for Him.

Whoever reflects on this meaning in the Qur'an will be led into gardens of knowledge that Allah has protected from every liar who turns away from the Book of Allah and from drawing guidance from it. Even if this book of ours contained only this section, it would suffice for one who has taste and recognition. And Allah is the Granter of success in what is correct.

((End of the nineteenth part))

(Section)
Among His names is "the King" (al-Malik). The true meaning of kingship belongs to Him, Glorified is He, in every respect, and this attribute necessarily entails all the other attributes of perfection. For it is impossible for complete and true kingship to be established for one who has no life, no power, no will, no hearing, no sight, no speech, and no voluntary action proceeding from him. How can one be described as a king who does not command or forbid, does not reward or punish, does not give or withhold, does not honour or abase, does not humble or dignify, does not bestow favour or take vengeance, does not raise or lower, does not send messengers to the regions of his kingdom, and does not direct his servants with his commands and prohibitions? What true kingship is there for one who lacks all of that? This shows that those who deny His names and attributes (al-mu'attilah) have made His subjects more perfect than He is, and one of them would be averse to having his own command and kingship described in the way he describes his Lord. Thus the attribute of divine kingship necessitates the existence of what the exercise of kingship cannot be complete without, and all of it comes from Him, Glorified is He. So the perfection of His kingship does not depend on anything other than Him, for everything else is attributed to Him and depends for its existence on His will and His creation.

(Section)
Ibn al-Qayyim said, after some discussion:
Once you understand these two points, applying the name "al-Salam" (the Giver of Peace, the Free from Imperfection) to God as one of His names is more fitting than all of that and more deserving of this name than any other bearer of it, because He, Glorified is He, is free from every defect and deficiency in every respect. He is the true Peace in every sense, whereas the created being is peaceful only in a relative sense. He, Glorified is He, is "Peace" in His essence, free from every defect and deficiency one might imagine; He is "Peace" in His attributes, free from every defect and deficiency; and He is "Peace" in His actions, free from every defect, evil, injustice, or act that occurs without wisdom. Rather, He is the true Peace in every respect and in every sense. It is thus known that His deserving this name is more complete than the deserving of anything else to which it is applied. This is the reality of the transcendence (tanzih) with which He has declared Himself transcendent and with which His Messenger declared Him transcendent. He is "Peace" from having a consort or a child, "Peace" from having an equal, a peer, a namesake, or a like, and "Peace" from having a partner. Therefore, when you consider the individual attributes of His perfection, you will find that each attribute is a "peace" from what contradicts its perfection. His life is peace from death, from drowsiness and sleep. Likewise His self-subsistence (qayyumiyyah) and His power are peace from fatigue and weariness. His knowledge is peace from anything being absent from it, from the onset of forgetfulness, or from any need for recollection or reflection. His will is peace from departing from wisdom and benefit. His words are peace from falsehood and injustice; indeed His words are complete in truthfulness and justice. His self-sufficiency (ghina) is peace from any need for another in any respect; rather everything else is in need of Him while He is free from everything other than Him. His kingship is peace from any contender for it, any partner, any helper who is a supporter, or any intercessor with Him without His permission. His divinity is peace from any partner in it; rather He is Allah, there is no god but He. His forbearance, pardon, forgiveness, and overlooking are peace from being due to any need of His, or to any flattery, or to any obsequiousness, as happens with others; rather they are pure generosity, benevolence, and munificence. Likewise His punishment, vengeance, severity of seizing, and swiftness of retribution are peace from being injustice, gloating, harshness, or cruelty; rather they are pure wisdom, justice, and the placing of things in their proper places. These too deserve praise and thanks just as His benevolence, reward, and blessings do. Indeed, if He were to place reward where punishment belongs, that would contradict His wisdom and His might. So His placing punishment where it belongs is part of His justice, wisdom, and might.

He is peace from what His enemies and those ignorant of Him imagine of contradiction to His wisdom, His decree, and His destiny. He is peace from futility, oppression, and injustice, and from the supposition that anything occurs contrary to His profound wisdom, and from His legislation and His religion. He is peace from contradiction, disagreement, instability, and anything contrary to the benefit and mercy of His servants, to doing good to them, and to His wisdom. Rather, all of His legislation is wisdom, mercy, benefit, and justice. Likewise, His giving is peace from being an exchange or from any need of the giver; and His withholding is peace from stinginess and fear of poverty. Rather, His giving is pure benevolence, not for exchange nor out of need, and His withholding is pure justice and wisdom, unmixed with stinginess or incapacity.

His istiwa' (rising) and His exaltation over His Throne are peace from being in need of what would bear Him or what He would rise upon. Rather, the Throne is in need of Him, and its bearers are in need of Him; He is free of the Throne, of its bearers, and of everything other than Him. His istiwa' and His exaltation are not confined by any limit, nor by any need for a Throne or anything else, nor by anything encompassing Him, Glorified and Exalted is He. Rather, He was (and there was no Throne), and He had no need of it, and He is the Self-Sufficient, the Praiseworthy. His istiwa' over His Throne and His dominion over His creation are among the requirements of His kingship and His subjugation, without any need for an accident or anything else in any respect. His descent every night to the lowest heaven is peace from what contradicts His exaltation, and peace from what contradicts His self-sufficiency. His perfection is peace from everything that a denier (mu'attil) or an anthropomorphist (mushabbih) might imagine. It is peace from ever being beneath anything or confined within anything.

Exalted is our Lord above everything that contradicts His perfection, His self-sufficiency, His hearing, and His sight, peace from everything that the anthropomorphist imagines or the denier invents, and His allegiance to His friends (muwalah).

It is peace from His allegiance being like the allegiance of one created to another created. Rather, it is an allegiance of mercy, goodness, benevolence, and kindness, as He said: ﴿And say: "Praise be to God, who has not taken a son, and who has no partner in the dominion, and who has no protecting friend out of weakness."﴾

So He did not negate that He may have a friend absolutely; rather He negated that He have a friend out of weakness. Likewise His love for those who love Him and for His friends is peace from the accidents of a created being's love for another created being, such as being love from need, or flattery, or benefit from being near to them. It is also peace from what the deniers say about it. Likewise what He attributed to Himself, such as a hand and a face: it is peace from what the anthropomorphist imagines or the denier invents.

So reflect on how His name "al-Salam" comprises all that He has declared Himself transcendent of, Blessed and Exalted is He. How many are those who have memorized this name without knowing what these secrets and meanings it contains. And God is the One sought for help, and the One asked to grant success in commenting on the Most Beautiful Names in this manner; He is near and responsive.

For when a palm tree grows tall and rises, beyond the reach of hands, it is called jabbarah. For this reason He, Glorified is He, made His name al-Jabbar paired with al-'Aziz (the Mighty) and al-Mutakabbir, and each of these three names includes the other two.

These three names are parallel to three other names: (al-Khaliq, al-Bari', al-Musawwir: the Creator, the Originator, the Fashioner). So al-Jabbar and al-Mutakabbir operate as an elaboration of the meaning of the name al-'Aziz, just as al-Bari' and al-Musawwir are an elaboration of the meaning of the name al-Khaliq. Thus al-Jabbar among His attributes returns to the perfection of power, might, and dominion, and for this reason it is among His Most Beautiful Names.

As for the created being, his being described as jabbar is a blame and a deficiency, as God, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Thus God seals every heart of a proud tyrant﴾ [Ghafir: 35].

And God, Exalted is He, said to His Messenger ﷺ: ﴿You are not over them a jabbar﴾ [Qaf: 45], i.e., one who dominates them, compelling and forcing them to belief.

In al-Tirmidhi and others, from the Prophet ﷺ: "The tyrants and the arrogant will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection in the form of ants, trampled upon by people."

As for "al-Khaliq" (the Creator) and "al-Musawwir" (the Fashioner): if they are used absolutely, without qualification, they are applied only to the Lord, as in His saying: ﴿the Creator, the Originator, the Fashioner﴾. If they are used with a qualification, they may be applied to a servant, as one says to someone who measures something out for its cutting: that he creates it. A poet said:

"And you indeed cut what you have created, while some people create and then do not cut."

Ibn al-Qayyim's commentary on surah 59, verses 23–24 (part 2 of 2):

That is, you have a power by which you carry out and execute what you have decreed in yourself and in others. Someone may decree things while being unable to carry them out and enforce them. In this sense, it is valid to apply the term "creator" (khaliq) to a servant, in the words of the Exalted: ﴿So blessed is Allah, the best of creators﴾.

That is, the best of those who shape and those who determine. The Arabs say "qaddartu al-adim wa khalaqtuhu" ("I measured the leather and cut it") when one measures a hide in order to cut from it a water-skin, a waterskin (qirba), or the like.

Mujahid said: "They create, and Allah creates, and Allah is the best of creators."

Al-Layth said: "A man who is a khaliq is one who makes (sani'), and the women are al-khaliqat."

Muqatil said: "The Exalted says: He is better in creation than those who make images and other things, of which nothing moves. As for al-Bari' (the Originator), it is not valid to apply it to anyone except Him, the Glorified, for He is the one who originated (bara'a) creation and brought it into being after it was non-existent."

The servant's power does not extend to that, for the furthest reach of his capacity is to manipulate some attributes of what the Lord, the Exalted, has brought into being and originated, and to change them from one state to another in a specific manner beyond which his power does not extend.

Not from this category is "bara'tu al-qalam" (I trimmed the pen), because it is a defective (mu'tall) root, not a hamzated one; nor is "bara'tu min al-maradh" (I recovered from the illness), because it is an intransitive verb, not transitive. Likewise, "mubdi' al-shay'" (the originator of a thing) and "badi'uhu" (its innovator/wonderful maker) are not valid to apply except to the Lord, as in His saying: ﴿Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾.

Ibداع (al-ibda', innovation/origination) is bringing a thing into being without a precedent example. A servant is called mubtadi' (an innovator) because he has introduced a statement that was not practiced by the Sunnah. Then whoever follows him in it is also called mubtadi'.

(Benefit)

Know that He, the Glorified, uses His names to prove His oneness and to negate association with Him. Had these been names without meaning, they would not indicate this, as in the saying of Harun to the worshippers of the calf: ﴿O my people, you are only being tested by it, and indeed your Lord is the Most Merciful﴾ [Ta-Ha: 90].

And His saying, in the same story: ﴿Your god is only Allah, other than whom there is no deity, who has encompassed all things in knowledge﴾ [Ta-Ha: 98].

And His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And your God is one God; there is no deity except Him, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate﴾ [al-Baqarah: 163].

And His saying, the Glorified, at the end of Surah al-Hashr: ﴿He is Allah, other than whom there is no deity, the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed; He is the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. He is Allah, other than whom there is no deity, the King, the Pure, the Source of Peace, the Granter of Security, the Guardian, the Mighty, the Compeller, the Superior. Glory be to Allah above what they associate with Him﴾ [al-Hashr: 22–23].

So "sabbaha" (glorified) means He declared Himself free of the associations of the polytheists with Him, right after praising Himself with His most beautiful names, which necessitate His oneness and the impossibility of affirming a partner for Him.

Whoever reflects on this meaning in the Qur'an will be led into gardens of knowledge that Allah has protected from every liar who turns away from the Book of Allah and from drawing guidance from it. Even if this book of ours contained only this section, it would suffice for one who has taste and recognition. And Allah is the Granter of success in what is correct.

((End of the nineteenth part))
